keV sterile neutrino Dark Matter Alexander Merle
1. Introduction
If there is one thing the astro- and/or particle physics communities agree on, it is that one of
the major questions of contemporary science is about the true nature of Dark Matter (DM). This
substance makes up more than 80% of the full matter content of the Universe, but up to now we
have not yet ﬁgured out what is behind. While we are somewhat certain of several aspects of DM
(its energy density, its rough distribution today, and the fact that it was crucial for cosmic structure
formation), there are other things we do not know precisely (its identity, its production mechanism,
its momentum distribution after production). While there are strong hints towards DM being made
out of new elementary particles, our partial lack of knowledge suggests that we should question old
believes and possibly re-evaluate certain statements made in the literature.
In the literature, the “standard” candidate for DM is regarded to be a Weakly Interacting Mas-
sive Particle (WIMP). However, while WIMPs do have a lot of theory motivation behind them, we
cannot ignore the fact that we have not yet seen an unambiguous signal. On the contrary, on-going
experiments push our limits further and further, such that, given the lack of a detection, we must
start to seriously consider alternative possibilities.
Taking a step back, we should ask which non-WIMP particle ticks all the boxes for DM. One
natural candidate is a sterile neutrino N . This particle with mass mN is electrically neutral and
interacts even more feebly than an “active” neutrino να (with ﬂavours α = e, µ, τ), namely by
vertices suppressed by the small active-sterile mixing angle θα. Given that sterile neutrinos can be
rather massive, they would certainly be able to act as DM, provided that they are produced in the
early Universe in the right amount and with a suitable momentum spectrum [1].
Before we start, let us remark that the most complete source of information and references in
existence at the moment is the White Paper on keV sterile neutrino Dark Matter [2].
2. Non-thermal DM production and how to produce keV sterile neutrinos
Studying the literature, one ﬁnds a very common statement about sterile neutrino DM which
is, however, only correct in a tiny fraction of all cases. The prejudice is that sterile neutrino DM
would be warm. The origin of this statement is in parts historic, but when looking at the details it is
often just not the case. Formally, a thermal distribution would amount to the following momentum
spectrum,

tion constraints on an example model parameter space (right), see [4].
For the case of keV sterile neutrinos, several production mechanisms are discussed, out of
which all but the very last one do exhibit non-thermal spectra:
• non-resonant production: First studied by Langacker [ 4], linked to DM by Dodelson and
Widrow [5]. Detailed computations are of a newer date [ 6, 7]. This mechanism nowadays
known to be excluded by observations.
• resonant production: First studied by Enqvist and collaborators [8], linked to DM by Shi and
Fuller [9]. Detailed computations are of a newer date [ 6, 10]. This mechanism is allowed
(but constrained) by observations.
• (scalar) decay production: Several studies are available (see, e.g., Refs. [11, 12] for different
cases of parent particles). This mechanism is in good agreement with observations.
• thermal overproduction with subsequent entropy dilution: Discussed for keV sterile neutri-
nos in [14]. Non-trivial to get in agreement with Big Bang Nucleosynthesis.
Out of these, the second and third mechanisms are discussed most frequently, which is why we will
put our main focus on those two here.
2

--- Page 4 ---
keV sterile neutrino Dark Matter Alexander Merle
3. Production of keV sterile neutrinos by active-sterile mixing
The most natural approach is to produce sterile neutrinos by their admixture to the active-
neutrino sector [ 4, 5, 6, 7], which exploits the fact that any reaction producing active neutrinos
can also produce steriles – only with a much smaller probability – as long as some active-sterile
mixing angles are non-zero. This could gradually produce enough sterile neutrinos to explain the
observed amount of DM, but the resulting spectrum would feature too many particles with rather
large momenta, making this setting similar to a hot DM case and thus excluded by data.
However, this could change for the case of a lepton number asymmetry being present in the
early Universe, a suitable value of which can resonantly enhance the transitions from active to
sterile neutrinos [6, 8, 9, 10]. While the origin of such an asymmetry has to be explained at ﬁrst,
its effects have been computed. Basically, if the asymmetry is large enough, it produces very
many sterile neutrinos at a very speciﬁc combination of momentum and temperature. Thus, in the
momentum distribution function, a sharp peak appears on top of a continuous spectrum, clearly
comprising a non-thermal distribution. If this peak is located at a comparatively small momentum,
i.e., a big fraction of the sterile neutrinos are not very fast, the resulting spectrum should be “cooler”
(i.e., smaller momenta are more dominant) than the one resulting from non-resonant production.
It is non-trivial to obtain statements from cosmic structure formation about non-thermal spec-
tra, cf. left Fig. 1, so that new methods have to be developed to do so. Confronting resonant
production with data, it turns out that the “coldest” region, which would be closest to the cold DM
case, is located in a region of the parameter space that is by far excluded from the X-ray bound (i.e.,
from not observing the photons stemming from sterile neutrino DM decay,N→ νγ ). All parameter
combinations that are left can be investigated to see whether they are compatible with cosmic struc-
ture formation. This has been done in Ref. [15], using a modiﬁed version of the so-called extended
Press-Schechter approach. Two methods have been applied to the spectra resulting from resonant
production: halo counting (i.e., whether a given DM distribution produces at least as many small
haloes as dwarf galaxies are observed) and the Lyman-α method (i.e., whether the distribution of
the intergalactic medium coincides with the DM distribution expected from the spectrum under
consideration). The result was that, contrary to some statements in the literature which did not take
into account bounds from structure formation, resonant production is pushed already by current
data. Thus, depending on how aggressively the Lyman- α data is interpreted, resonant production
may even be completely excluded. However, it is in any case correct to say that structure formation
does yield a strong constraint on this production mechanism, cf. Fig. 2.
4. Production of keV sterile neutrinos by particle decays
Production by particle decays is an alternative way to generate keV sterile neutrino DM, by
ﬁrst producing a parent particle (e.g., a singlet scalar S) which then decays into sterile neutrinos
(e.g., S→ NN). Typically, the decisive parameters are the Higgs portal coupling λ, which drives
the production of the scalar from Standard Model particles, and the Yukawa coupling y, which
drives the decay. Depending on whether the scalar itself equilibrates [ 11] or not [ 12], different
(non-thermal) spectra are possible, some resembling e.g. the green curve plotted in the left Fig. 1.
3

--- Page 5 ---
keV sterile neutrino Dark Matter Alexander Merle
The currently most advanced analysis of such cases has been presented in the last Ref. [ 12],
which also confronted the resulting cases with cosmic structure formation. A resulting snapshot
of the allowed parameter space, for the case of a scalar mass of mS = 500 GeV , is depicted in
the right Fig. 1. Here, the right (left) part of the plot corresponds to the region of large (small)
λ or, in other words, where the scalar freezes out (freezes in) before decaying. In this plot, the
lines of correct abundance (regions of sizable but too low abundance) are indicated by the solid
red/purple/blue lines (bands) for different sterile neutrino masses. In both cases, the red parts are
forbidden by the Lyman-α data. Other bounds, such as the Tremaine-Gunn or overclosure bounds
are also displayed, along with indirect collider bounds from unitarity and from the W-boson mass
correction (the latter two of which however only play a role in the most minimal setting possible).
A detailed analysis conﬁrms the picture given. Decay production is, in general, less constraint
by (and thus in better agreement with) cosmic structure formation, as can also be seen from Fig. 2.
This statement remains true even if, after DM production by decays is completed, non-resonant
production produces a late-time correction to the spectrum [7].
Even more interestingly, on top of being the production mechanism with the better agreement
with data, decay production can lead to very involved spectra with two or partially even three dif-
ferent characteristic momentum scales. This feature can possibly be used to address the (in)famous
small scale problems of cosmic structure formation, i.e., the missing satellite, too-big-to-fail, and
cusp-core problems. In order to derive bounds (e.g. from the Lyman- α forrest), the last Ref. [ 12]
developed a completely new method based on the computation of the so-called squared transfer
function T 2(k), which encodes information on which structures (i.e., of which size 2π/k) in space
are suppressed compared to the cold DM case. This method consists of checking whether the part
of the transfer function above the half-mode T 2 = 1/2 is allowed by the Lyman-α data, or not, and
it turns out to be extremely robust. Indeed, the green lines shown in the right Fig. 1 arise from an
alternative bound related to structure formation, namely the abundance of highly redshifted (i.e.,
distant) galaxies. This bound derives from completely different physics but, while it is slight less
stringent, it basically tracks the boundary between the red and purple regions, and thus strongly
supports the results obtained in the last Ref. [12].
5. Conclusions and outlook
We end by looking at the current situation of keV sterile neutrino DM. In Fig. 2, we have
collected many current limits. First of all, the most stringent limits exist on the active-sterile mixing
(collectively labeled θ here, because not all the limits may apply to all generations of fermions).
Clearly, for large masses, the X-ray bound (green) is the strongest, due to the rate of the N→ νγ
decay depending on the mass mN to the ﬁfth power. For smaller masses, though, the superior
bound is the one stemming from not overproducing the DM by non-resonant production (yellow).
Other bounds, such as those from reionisation (blue), dark radiation (red dotted), or the lifetime
(black dashed), conﬁrm the stronger bounds but cannot compete with them. From the other side,
cosmic structure formation is the strongest driving force to constrain mN. There exists a general
lower bound on the sterile neutrino mass (Tremaine-Gunn bound, gray rectangle), stemming from
the mere fact that sterile neutrinos are fermions, applied to the cores of galaxies. When taking
into account information about the production mechanism, this bound can be strongly improved.

observe dwarf galaxies, we can in fact obtain very stringent constraints on the different production
mechanisms. As can be seen from the plot, resonant production is in fact rather pushed by current
constraints, for the reasons explained in Sec. 3, while scalar decay production, Sec. 4, seems in
better shape. Note that, in both cases, the spectra closest to the cold DM limit have been chosen,
which is a rather conservative approach.

Figure 2: Summary plot of current constraints and future experimental reaches.
The ways forward in this ﬁeld should be clear from the plot. First and foremost, obviously,
if our data on cosmic structures and, related to that, our understanding of cosmic structure for-
mation in general improves, this may enable us to discriminate between different early Universe
production mechanisms. Of course, another direction that should be pushed for is to continue hunt-
ing for the smoking gun X-ray signature stemming from DM decay. While the hopes were high
for the Hitomi satellite, it was lost in 2016 through a chain of unfortunate events. Other searches
such as NuSTAR (pink) can improve the limits – however, due to many unknowns involved, one
must be careful not to overstate these advances (as, e.g., done in the ﬁrst version of the NuSTAR
paper [16], which incorrectly stated that it would be closing in on the entire parameter space of
sterile neutrino DM, while in reality it only does so for resonant production). Finally, there are also
ground-based experiments trying to constrain active-sterile mixing. While several attempts such as
KATRIN/TRISTAN [17], ECHo [ 18], or DyNO [ 19] are on their way, they unfortunately do not
seem to be able to compete with astrophysical/cosmological limits.
Nevertheless, this ﬁeld clearly offers both, sufﬁcient parameter space available and means
to probe it – plus a well-motivated non-thermal DM candidate which may in particular strongly
impact on cosmic structure formation. We can be curious what the future holds for this ﬁeld.

args.claim: f-012 re-supported verbatim from XRISM 2510.24560 abstract: "We stack 3.75 Megaseconds of early XRISM Resolve observations of ten galaxy clusters to search for unidentified spectral lines in the E= 2.5-15 keV band (rest frame)... No unidentified lines are detected... with the 3σ upper limit on the m_s∼7.1 keV DM particle decay rate (which corresponds to a E= 3.55 keV emission line) of Γ∼1.0×10^-27 s^-1. This upper limit is 3−4 times lower than the one derived by Hitomi ... but still 5 times higher than the XMM-Newton detection reported by Bulbul et al. (2014)". args.claim: f-013 partially re-supported, but the requested figure readings were not obtained. Verbatim from 2405.17861: Eq. 2 reads "Γγ = 9/1024 α/π^4 G_F^2 m_s^5 sin^2 2θ = 1.36×10^-22 (m_s/1keV)^5 sin^2 2θ s^-1". The exponent -22 is correct as written, because sin^2 2θ is not normalized there; it equals 1.36e-32 s^-1 at sin^2 2θ = 1e-10, so the board's "correction to 1e-32" applies only to the normalized form. The paper places "new upper limits on the active-sterile mixing angle θ for sterile neutrino masses m_s = 6−40 keV" at 95% CL. Fig. 3 is plotted on a sin^2(2θ) axis from 1e-15 to 1e-10. The paper says that observed limits are "stronger ... in certain mass ranges (e.g. m_νs = 8−9 keV or 23−25 keV)", and that "the borderline excess at 40 keV is the known instrumental effect". I could not read numerical values at 7, 10 or 20 keV: Fig. 3 is missing from the HTML rendering, and the Fig. 1 image (registered as Figure 15) was downloaded but cannot be digitized with the available tools. So the only NuSTAR number per mass is the secondary 2507.18752 summary, sin^2 2θ <~ 1e-12 across 6-40 keV.

The sterile neutrino dark matter’s large mixing angle in low-reheating scenarios is much more accessible
to laboratory experiments like β-decay [139, 140, 132]. There are also eﬀorts at testing these couplings via
K-capture experiments [141, 142] including novel methods employing atom traps that search for the massive
admixed neutrino in nuclear beta decay via complete kinematic reconstruction of the ﬁnal state [141, 143].
5.3. Non-oscillation Production: Particle Decays
In addition to the non-resonant and resonant oscillation production models, a few other production
mechanisms have been proposed via particle decays. For most cases, a generic scalarS-particle is introduced
with an interaction Lagrangian
Lint = y
2(νR)cνRS +h.c. (45)
S-particles are created in some process in the early Universe and could decay into sterile neutrinos at some
later point. Clearly, the abundance is now independent of the active-sterile mixing angle, but in general, if
this mechanism is responsible for the bulk of production, the mixing angle must be below that produced by
non-resonant thermal production. In addition, depending on the nature of the mechanism, the scalar-decay
sterile neutrino dark matter could be “warmer” or “colder” than in oscillation production. A thorough
review of these production mechanisms is given in Ref. [60], and we provide a brief overview here.
Regardless of the mechanism, if the active-sterile mixing is large enough for Dodelson-Widrow or Shi-
Fuller production to be signiﬁcant, that has to be included. In the various particle-decay mechanisms,
the “parent” S-particle can itself be in or out of thermal equilibrium at the time the sterile neutrinos are
produced. The decay into the sterile neutrino dark matter has been considered via several scalar particles as a
single particle decay channel or via one part of multiple possible decay channels [144, 21, 145, 146, 147, 148].
In scalar decay cases, the production of sterile neutrinos is governed by a Boltzmann kinetic equation
describing their distribution f(p,t ) as a function of momentum p and time t [144]

5.2. Low Reheating Temperature Universe and the Visible Sterile Neutrino
One possibility in the case of oscillation-based production is that the Universe never heated up to the
full peak-production temperatures of the given production mechanism. In this case, large mixing angles
can produce the proper production levels because of the reduction of the level of a strong thermal bath.
This possibility was proposed in Gelmini et al. [127]. Such low reheating scenarios can under-produce the
cosmological relativistic energy density measured as the eﬀective number of neutrinos,Neﬀ, but for reheating
temperatures of TR = 5 MeV, Neﬀ can be within 10% of its canonical value, which remains consistent with
current measures ofNeﬀ = 3.15±0.23 (1σ) [128]. Future CMB experiments are forecast place stronger limits
on the relativistic energy density, asNeﬀ, to within∼1% [129]. Though low reheating temperature universes
are an unusual cosmology, they are possible, with baryogenesis occurring at low scale via an Aﬄeck-Dine
mechanism [130]. Perhaps most interestingly is that this plausible scenario marries quite disparate ﬁelds
of cosmological dark matter production, cosmological large scale structure constraints on hot dark matter
(HDM), galaxy formation limits on WDM and mixed WDM plus CDM, Type II supernova reheating models,
as well as laboratory-based nuclear beta-decay searches and neutrinoless double beta decay searches.

args.claim:
Final viability table in the (m_s, sin^2 2θ) plane:
- DW (non-resonant): not viable as all of the dark matter. The DM line sits at sin^2 2θ = 2.55e-10 (7.1 keV), 1.37e-10 (10 keV), 3.9e-11 (20 keV) and 7.6e-12 (50 keV) (server normalization, f-008). All of these lie above the XRISM limit (~4e-10 at 7.1 keV is the only point below the line's value there, but it sits within a factor of 1.6) and above the NuSTAR <~1e-12 and SPI <~3e-14 limits. Binding constraint: X-ray. BBN is not binding; Delta chi^2 < 0.15 along the line. Provenance: f-008 and f-014 to f-017. 2507.18752 states "the original DW mechanism is ruled out as producing the entirety of the dark matter".
- Shi-Fuller with L >~ 0.5 at T > 20 MeV: viable at m_s >~ 10 keV and sin^2 2θ <~ 1e-14. Binding constraints are X-ray (NuSTAR 1e-12, SPI 3e-14 above 40 keV) and structure formation (m_th > 8.4-8.5 keV from galaxy counts and lensing, against a Lyman-alpha preference of 4.1 keV). Provenance: verbatim quotes from 2507.18752 (f-014). Server BBN is trivially allowed (f-003), but this is not an independent test because the tool caps L at 0.1.
- Flavor-dependent asymmetry (2502.17374): lighter m_s at smaller mixing, with BBN limits weakened and colder spectra. Abstract only; no numerical ranges are quoted. Saturation at large L (2609.31340) leaves a window of about two decades in sin^2 2θ; abstract only.
- Reheating (inflaton decay, BR <~ 1e-4; 2601.03346): cold DM at mixings below the X-ray limits. Binding constraint: X-ray only. Abstract only.

delta:
**Completed — Re-extract the quantitative literature claims (f-002, f-012, f-013) as verbatim quotes. Build a verified X-ray limit table at m_s = 7.1, 10, 20, 40 and 50 keV. Then produce the final per-mechanism viability table in the (m_s, sin^2 2theta) plane (DW, Shi-Fuller with lepton asymmetry, flavor-dependent asymmetry, reheating production), with a provenance column for each entry..** All three contested findings now have verbatim quotes. The X-ray limit table covers five masses, but only one value is read directly from a primary source; the rest come from a secondary summary. Viability table: f-018. Findings f-014 to f-018 and dead end x-02 are posted.

(1) f-002, re-supported by f-014, quoting the 2507.18752 full text (runs/261021_110150/2507.18752.txt, tc-...-w2-d-05-72). Viable region: 'L≳0.5 ... m_s≳10 keV and sin^2(2θ)≲10^-14'. NuSTAR: 'sin^2(2θ)≲10^-12 in the 6–40 keV mass range'. INTEGRAL/SPI: 'exclude lifetimes below ∼10^20 s at 95% CL [corresponding to sin^2(2θ)≲3×10^-14] in the ≳40 keV mass regime'. Structure formation: m_th > 8.4 keV from galaxy counts, m_th > 8.5 keV from counts plus strong lensing, and a Lyman-alpha preference of m_th = 4.1 (+33.3/-1.5) keV.

(2) f-012, re-supported by f-015, quoting the 2510.24560 abstract (tc-...-84). XRISM stacked 3.75 Ms of data on ten clusters over 2.5-15 keV. Its 3-sigma limit is Γ ∼ 1.0e-27 s^-1 at m_s ∼ 7.1 keV, which converts to sin^2 2θ < ~4e-10 (my conversion, not a quote).

(3) f-013, partly re-supported and downgraded to medium by f-016 (tc-...-77, -80, -85). Eq. 2 of 2405.17861 reads 1.36×10^-22 (m_s/keV)^5 sin^2 2θ s^-1. That exponent is correct as written, because sin^2 2θ is not normalised there; it equals 1.36e-32 s^-1 at sin^2 2θ = 1e-10. The paper gives 95% limits for m_s = 6-40 keV, with observed limits stronger than expected at 8-9 and 23-25 keV and an instrumental excess at 40 keV. Fig. 3 is missing from the HTML rendering. The Fig. 1 image was downloaded (Figure 15, figures_2405.17861/fig01.png) but not read numerically. So the 7, 10 and 20 keV entries rest on the secondary summary value of <~1e-12. 2405.17861 is now cited in references.bib under arxiv240517861 (tc-...-96).

(4) X-ray limit table (f-017), cross-checked with the server's line tool:
- 7.1 keV: XRISM < ~4e-10 (3 sigma); NuSTAR <~1e-12.
- 10 keV: NuSTAR <~1e-12. At 1e-12 the tool gives Γ = 1.36e-29 s^-1, E = 5 keV and lifetime 7.35e28 s, not excluded by its tables (tc-...-95).
- 20 keV: NuSTAR <~1e-12. The tool's own tables exclude 1e-12 (d-02).
- 40 keV: the upper edge of NuSTAR coverage, where SPI <~3e-14 takes over.
- 50 keV: SPI <~3e-14. At 3e-14 the tool gives Γ = 1.28e-27 s^-1 and lifetime 7.8e26 s, not excluded (tc-...-94).
Warning: the SPI quote equates a lifetime of ~1e20 s with a mixing of 3e-14, but the tool gives 7.8e26 s at that mixing, a gap of about 7 orders of magnitude. The SPI mixing value needs checking against the primary SPI paper. My search for a 2024-2026 SPI or NuSTAR limit above 40 keV found nothing (dead end x-02, tc-...-86).

(5) Viability table (f-018):
- Dodelson-Widrow: excluded as all of the dark matter. Its dark-matter line (2.55e-10 at 7.1 keV, 1.37e-10 at 10 keV, 3.9e-11 at 20 keV, 7.6e-12 at 50 keV; server normalisation from f-008) lies above the NuSTAR and SPI limits, so X-ray is the binding constraint and BBN is not. Correction to the wording in f-018: at 7.1 keV the dark-matter line (2.55e-10) sits below the XRISM limit (~4e-10), so XRISM alone does not exclude it there; NuSTAR does.
- Shi-Fuller with L >~ 0.5 at T > 20 MeV: viable at m_s >~ 10 keV and sin^2 2θ <~ 1e-14. The binding constraints are X-ray and m_th. Provenance is the 2507.18752 quotes; the server cannot test this because it caps L at 0.1.
- Flavor-dependent asymmetry (2502.17374) and saturation at large L (2609.31340): lighter masses at smaller mixing, and about a two-decade window in mixing. Abstract only.
- Reheating production (2601.03346, branching ratio <~ 1e-4): cold dark matter below the X-ray limits. Abstract only.

args.claim: On the DW DM line, the standard DW-to-thermal mapping m_s = 4.43 keV (m_th/keV)^(4/3) (Viel et al. 2005, astro-ph/0501562; text downloaded, but the formula was not quoted verbatim from it) gives m_th = 0.75 keV (m_s = 3 keV), 1.42 keV (7.1 keV), 1.84 keV (10 keV), 3.10 keV (20 keV) and 6.16 keV (50 keV). Lyman-alpha m_th > 4 (6) keV requires m_s > 28 (48) keV, and satellite counts m_th > 8.4 keV require m_s > 76 keV. At m_s >= 28 keV the DW line has sin^2 2theta ~ 3e-10 (published normalization) or about 1e-11 (server). Both values lie far above the NuSTAR ceiling of about 1e-12 at 6-40 keV and the SPI ceiling of about 3e-14 above 40 keV (f-002). The surviving DW mass interval is therefore empty under all three normalizations.
args.note: The 4.43 keV (m_th)^(4/3) coefficient is the commonly used Viel+2005 value. I did not read or quote it verbatim from the downloaded text, so someone should confirm it there. The 50 keV DW point under the server normalization (7.6e-12) is above the SPI limit of 3e-14 by more than 100x.

args.claim: BBN robustness check. I used linearized f-009 slopes (dYp/dN_eff = 0.0135, dD/H/dN_eff = 0.331e-5) about the server SM values (Yp = 0.246815, D/H = 2.4433e-5). The 95% upper bounds on Delta N_eff are given as Delta chi^2 = 3.84 against the SM, with Delta chi^2 = 3.84 against the best fit in brackets. Brief data (Yp 0.245 +/- 0.003, D/H 2.53 +/- 0.03): Yp-only 0.32; D/H-only 0.58 [0.44]; combined 0.47 [0.37]. Server data (Yp 0.2449 +/- 0.004, D/H 2.547 +/- 0.025): Yp-only 0.46; D/H-only 0.66 [0.46]; combined 0.61 [0.43]. The server tool reports 0.548. D/H alone prefers Delta N_eff = 0.26 (brief data) or 0.31 (server data) because the SM D/H sits 2.9 or 4.1 sigma low, so the bound depends on the baseline at the 0.1-0.2 level. Joint bound with dYp/dxi_e = -0.25, assuming D/H does not depend on xi_e, using 2-dof Delta chi^2 = 5.99. Brief data: Delta N_eff in [0.04, 0.48] and xi_e = 0.0073 + 0.054 Delta N_eff +/- 0.029. Server data: Delta N_eff in [0.13, 0.50] and xi_e = 0.0077 + 0.054 Delta N_eff +/- 0.039. So |xi_e| <~ 0.03-0.06 overall, and a positive xi_e of about 0.03 compensates Delta N_eff of about 0.5 in Yp.
args.note: These are analytic Gaussian calculations, not server runs. My linearized combined server-data bound (0.61) differs from the tool's 0.548, probably because the fit is nonlinear or the tool uses a different chi^2 convention. I neglected the D/H dependence on xi_e (dD/H/dxi_e).

delta: **Completed — Settle the factor-3 DW relic-density normalization against a published calculation and compute m_th along the DW dark-matter line. Also give a short BBN robustness check: the Delta N_eff bound under the brief's data versus the server's data, and the joint (Delta N_eff, xi_e) bound using dYp/dxi_e ~ -0.25..** Normalization (f-019): the published DW fit in arXiv:1705.01837 (Abazajian review) Eq. 37 is m_s ~ 3.40 keV (sin^2 2theta/1e-8)^-0.615 (Omega_DM/0.26)^0.5 x 0.527 erfc[-1.15 (T_QCD/170 MeV)^2.15]. It is cited in references.bib under key arxiv170501837. I inverted it by hand. Its dark-matter line sits at sin^2 2theta ~ 1.23e-8 (3 keV), 3.0e-9 (7.1 keV), 1.73e-9 (10 keV), 5.6e-10 (20 keV) and 1.26e-10 (50 keV). The QCD-era uncertainty (T_QCD 150-200 MeV) moves these by about +10%/-7%. The server line from predict_sterile_nu_grid (sterile_nu_grid_DW_2461e9.csv, Omega h^2 = 0.119-0.120) is 1.2e-9, 2.55e-10, 1.37e-10, 3.9e-11 and 7.6e-12. The published normalization therefore needs 10-17x more mixing than the server and 3.4-5.5x more than the brief's formula, and it scales differently with mass and mixing. Verdict at 7.1 keV (f-020): against the XRISM limit of about 4e-10, the server line (2.55e-10) survives, while the brief's line (7.65e-10) and the published line (3.0e-9) are excluded. Using the published normalization, DW at 7.1 keV is excluded by about 7.5x. m_th (f-021): I used the DW-to-thermal mapping m_s = 4.43 keV (m_th)^(4/3) from Viel+2005 (astro-ph/0501562). I downloaded that paper but did not quote the coefficient verbatim from it. This gives m_th = 0.75, 1.42, 1.84, 3.10 and 6.16 keV at m_s = 3, 7.1, 10, 20 and 50 keV. Lyman-alpha (m_th > 4-6 keV) then needs m_s > 28-48 keV, and satellite counts (m_th > 8.4 keV) need m_s > 76 keV. At those masses the DW line under any of the three normalizations sits well above the NuSTAR (~1e-12) and SPI (~3e-14) ceilings, so the surviving DW mass interval is empty. BBN (f-022): these are analytic results from linearized f-009 slopes, not server runs. Upper bounds on Delta N_eff at 95%, relative to the SM: with the brief's data, 0.32 from Yp only, 0.58 from D/H only and 0.47 combined. With the server's data, 0.46, 0.66 and 0.61. The server tool itself quotes 0.548. The SM D/H sits 2.9-4.1 sigma low, so D/H prefers Delta N_eff ~ 0.3 and the bound moves by 0.1-0.2 depending on the baseline. For the joint bound I used dYp/dxi_e = -0.25 and 2-dof Delta chi^2 < 5.99. Brief data: Delta N_eff in [0.04, 0.48], with xi_e = 0.0073 + 0.054 Delta N_eff +/- 0.029. Server data: Delta N_eff in [0.13, 0.50], with xi_e = 0.0077 + 0.054 Delta N_eff +/- 0.039. Overall |xi_e| <~ 0.03-0.06. Question q-09 is posted. Open items: the Viel coefficient and the full Eq. 37 citation still need verbatim quotes, and dD/H/dxi_e was neglected.

contested.reason: The tool values at 10 keV (Gamma 1.36e-29 s^-1, lifetime 7.35e28 s) and 50 keV (1.28e-27 s^-1, 7.84e26 s) match the excerpts. Two parts do not hold. (1) The 'not excluded' and 'excluded' verdicts at 10, 20 and 50 keV cannot be seen in the truncated excerpts. (2) The claimed 7-order inconsistency in the SPI quote is almost certainly a seconds-versus-years slip. The tool's own output at 50 keV and 3e-14 is 2.48e19 yr. Read as ~1e20 yr (3.2e27 s), the SPI lifetime matches sin^2 2theta ~2.3e-14 at 40 keV and ~7.5e-15 at 50 keV, which agrees with the quoted ~3e-14. The finding asserts a contradiction where the units are the more likely explanation.

The claim says the DW line at all masses lies 'above the XRISM limit', but at 7.1 keV the server line (2.55e-10) is below ~4e-10. # Sterile-neutrino dark matter after 2024: combining BBN and X-ray constraints on the (m_s, sin^2 2θ) plane

## Abstract

We combined tool-computed Big Bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) observables with published 2024–2026 X-ray and structure-formation limits to find which keV sterile-neutrino dark-matter regions survive. The sterile-neutrino server fits Yp, D/H and Li7 to the PRyMordial network.

For non-resonant (Dodelson–Widrow, DW) production, BBN is not a binding constraint. Along the Ω_s h² = 0.12 line the extra radiation is only ΔN_eff = 1e-4 to 1.1e-2, and |Δχ²_BBN| < 0.15. BBN excludes only mixings 40× (1 keV) to about 5000× (100 keV) larger than the dark-matter line. DW as all of the dark matter is excluded by X-ray limits combined with structure formation:

- The published DW normalization puts the 7.1 keV line at sin² 2θ ≈ 3.0e-9. That is about 7.5× above the XRISM-derived ceiling of about 4e-10.
- Lyman-alpha requires m_s ≳ 28–48 keV under DW. At those masses the DW line lies far above the NuSTAR (≲1e-12) and INTEGRAL/SPI (≲3e-14) ceilings.

What survives requires very small mixing. Resonant Shi–Fuller production with lepton asymmetry L ≳ 0.5 at T > 20 MeV gives m_s ≳ 10 keV and sin² 2θ ≲ 1e-14. Reheating or inflaton-decay production gives cold dark matter below the X-ray limits. Both rest on literature claims that our tools could not test independently.

## Background

The recent literature found is mostly about production mechanisms, not new X-ray datasets.

**Shi–Fuller resonant production.** Vogel, García Escudero, Froustey and Abazajian (arXiv:2507.18752) revisit this mechanism. They build on results that lepton asymmetries L_α ≳ 1 at T > 20 MeV are consistent with BBN. They state that "lepton asymmetries L≳0.5 at high temperatures open significant viable parameter space in the m_s≳10 keV and sin^2(2θ)≲10^-14 regime, compatible with both x-ray constraints from NuSTAR and INTEGRAL/SPI and recent Lyman-α inferences of m_th≈4.1 keV". The paper also uses:

-

a NuSTAR limit of sin²(2θ) ≲ 1e-12 over 6–40 keV;
- an INTEGRAL/SPI limit of sin²(2θ) ≲ 3e-14 at m_s ≳ 40 keV;
- structure bounds of m_th > 8.4 keV (galaxy counts) and m_th > 8.5 keV (counts plus strong lensing);
- a Lyman-alpha preference of m_th = 4.1 (+33.3/−1.5) keV.

It states that "the original DW mechanism is ruled out as producing the entirety of the dark matter".

**Variants of resonant production.** Gorbunov, Kalashnikov and Krugan (arXiv:2502.17374) argue that flavor-dependent asymmetries, which work best with inverted ordering, can cancel BBN limits on mixing and mass and give colder spectra. Gorbunov and Kalashnikov (arXiv:2609.31340, 2026) argue that a high flavor asymmetry saturates resonant production, leaving about a two-decade window in sin² 2θ. We confirmed that this paper exists. Its ID format had raised a concern that it was a hallucination.

**Reheating production.** Cline and Xu (arXiv:2601.03346, 2026) produce cold sterile-neutrino dark matter from inflaton decays with branching ratio ≲ 1e-4. This populates mixings below X-ray limits that oscillation production cannot reach.

**X-ray limits.**

- XRISM (arXiv:2510.24560) stacked 3.75 Ms on ten clusters and detected no unidentified lines over 2.5–15 keV.
- NuSTAR stray-light data over 11 years (Krivonos et al., arXiv:2405.17861) give 95% limits for m_s = 6–40 keV.
- Older context: the Chandra Galactic-bulge limit (arXiv:1905.00916), the eROSITA forecast (arXiv:1505.07829), and reviews (arXiv:1702.08430, arXiv:1705.01837).

**Lepton asymmetry and BBN at higher mass.** BBN constraints on heavy sterile neutrinos with lepton asymmetry appear in arXiv:2005.06721.

Shi–Fuller (SF) mode is crude. Its ΔN_eff is a heuristic set to 0.1 × the DW value. Its relic density is a fitting formula in L, capped at L = 0.1. The asymmetry is not fed into the BBN network.

Figure 6 shows Yp and D/H as functions of N_eff. A fully thermalized sterile state (N_eff = 4.044) gives Yp = 0.2596 and D/H × 1e5 = 2.777. BBN alone limits ΔN_eff < 0.548 at 95%. The linear slopes are dYp/dN_eff = 0.0135 and d(D/H × 1e5)/dN_eff = 0.331.

### BBN across the DW plane

A 100 × 100 DW scan covered m_s = 1–100 keV and sin² 2θ = 1e-15 to 1e-6. Of the 10,000 points, 1338 are BBN-excluded and 4300 overclose.

As a sanity check, the BEST short-baseline point (1.14 eV, sin² 2θ = 0.42) gives ΔN_eff = 1, Yp = 0.25956, D/H = 2.777e-5 and Δχ² = 23.1, so it is excluded. That is a 6.2σ tension with Planck and would be 33σ at CMB-S4.

### DW relic-density normalization

The server's DW relic formula is Ω_s h² = 0.1 (sin² 2θ/1e-9)(m_s/3 keV)^1.8. It was verified at three points:

- 3 keV and 1e-9 gives 0.100.
- 10 keV and 1e-9 gives 0.873.
- 1 keV and 1e-8 gives 0.138.

The exponent matches the brief's formula, but the normalization is 3× higher. The server's dark-matter line therefore sits at 3× smaller mixing than the brief's.

The published fit in the Abazajian review (arXiv:1705.01837, Eq. 37) is:

m_s ≈ 3.40 keV (sin² 2θ/1e-8)^−0.615 (Ω_DM/0.26)^0.5 × 0.527 erfc[−1.15 (T_QCD/170 MeV)^2.15]

We inverted it by hand. This inversion was not independently verified. The resulting dark-matter line is:

| m_s (keV) | Published line sin² 2θ | Server line sin² 2θ |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 1.23e-8 | 1.2e-9 |
| 7.1 | 3.0e-9 | 2.55e-10 |
| 10 | 1.73e-9 | 1.37e-10 |
| 20 | 5.6e-10 | 3.9e-11 |
| 50 | 1.26e-10 | 7.6e-12 |

QCD-era uncertainty (T_QCD = 150–200 MeV) moves the published values by about +10%/−7%. The published line needs 10× (3 keV) to 17× (50 keV) more mixing than the server, and 3.4–5.5× more than the brief's formula. It also has a different shape: Ω ∝ m² (sin² 2θ)^1.23. Server-based DW statements are therefore not c

onservative.

| 20 keV, 1e-12 | 4.36e-28 s⁻¹ | 4.42e-28 s⁻¹ | 10 keV | — |

Eq. 2 of arXiv:2405.17861 reads 1.36e-22 (m_s/keV)^5 sin² 2θ s⁻¹ with unnormalized mixing. That equals 1.36e-32 s⁻¹ at sin² 2θ = 1e-10, consistent with the formula above.

### X-ray limits by mass

**XRISM, 7.1 keV.** XRISM's 3σ limit is Γ ≈ 1.0e-27 s⁻¹ at m_s ≈ 7.1 keV. The paper says this is "3−4 times lower than the one derived by Hitomi … but still 5 times higher than the XMM-Newton detection reported by Bulbul et al. (2014)". The 3.55 keV line is therefore constrained but not ruled out. Scaling the tool's rate gives sin² 2θ ≲ 4e-10. This is our conversion, not a quoted value, and it uses the paper's cluster J-factors.

**NuSTAR, 6–40 keV.** The NuSTAR stray-light limits (arXiv:2405.17861) are plotted on a 1e-15 to 1e-10 axis. The paper says they "reach the bottom edge of theoretical predictions". The observed limits are stronger than expected at 8–9 and 23–25 keV, and the paper calls the "borderline excess at 40 keV" a known instrumental effect.

Figure 15 shows the paper's Fig. 1: the 95% NuSTAR stray-light limits on sin²(2θ) for the reference profile, compared with earlier NuSTAR and XMM bounds and theoretical lower bounds. **INTEGRAL/SPI and the unit problem.** arXiv:2507.18752 quotes SPI as excluding "lifetimes below ∼10^20 s" and equates this with sin² 2θ ≲ 3e-14. The tool's lifetime at that point is 7.8e26 s, about 7 orders of magnitude away. The critic judged it very likely that "1e20 s" should read 1e20 yr. The tool gives 2.48e19 yr at 50 keV and 3e-14, and m_s^5 scaling puts 1e20 yr at about 2.3e-14 at 40 keV. If so, the SPI ceiling is not flat at 3e-14. It tightens as m_s^−5 above 40 keV. This has not been checked against a primary SPI paper.

**Searches with no result.** No 2024–2026 eROSITA or INTEGRAL/SPI paper was found in any search. The eROSITA claim in the brief remains uncitable.

### DW at 7.1 keV: the verdict depends on normalization

Against the XRISM ceiling of about 4e-10, the outcome depends on which DW normalization is used:

| Normalization | DM line at 7.1 keV | Versus XRISM (~4e-10) |
|---|---|---|
| Server | 2.55e-10 | Survives |
| Brief's formula | 7.65e-10 | Excluded |
| Published (arXiv:1705.01837) | 3.0e-9 | Excluded by about 7.5× |

Taking the published fit as the reference, DW dark matter at 7.1 keV is excluded by XRISM alone. This co

nclusion relies on our hand inversion of the published fit, which the critic flagged as not independently checked. Under any normalization, NuSTAR's ≲ 1e-12 also excludes it, but that entry relies on the secondary summary.

### Structure formation along the DW line

We mapped DW mass to thermal-equivalent mass using m_s = 4.43 keV (m_th/keV)^(4/3), attributed to Viel et al. (astro-ph/0501562). The text was downloaded, but the coefficient was not quoted verbatim. The critic also notes an omitted (ω_DM/0.1225)^(−1/3) factor and 10–30% differences with newer mappings.

| m_s (keV) | m_th (keV) |
|---|---|
| 3 | 0.75 |
| 7.1 | 1.42 |
| 10 | 1.84 |
| 20 | 3.10 |
| 50 | 6.16 |

The structure-formation bounds then translate into DW mass bounds:

- Lyman-alpha (m_th > 4–6 keV) requires m_s > 28–48 keV.
- Satellite counts (m_th > 8.4 keV) require m_s > 76 keV.

At m_s ≥ 28 keV the DW line sits at about 3e-10 (published normalization) or about 1e-11 (server). Both are far above the NuSTAR and SPI ceilings, so the surviving DW mass interval is empty. The margin exceeds 100×, so the conclusion is robust to the mapping uncertainties.

### Resonant production in the tool

We ran SF mode at m_s = 10, 20 and 30 keV with sin² 2θ = 1e-14.

- BBN: ΔN_eff ≈ 1e-8 and Δχ² = 0. At 20 keV, Yp = 0.24682 and D/H = 2.4433e-5.
- Relic density: Ω_s h² = 0.122, 0.490 and 1.10 at L = 1e-3, and 1.22, 4.90 and 11.0 at L = 0.1. All points are flagged as overclosing.

These runs do not test arXiv:2507.18752:

- L is capped at 0.1, while the paper needs L ≳ 0.5.
- ΔN_eff is a heuristic.
- ξ_e is not fed into Yp.
- The SF relic density is not a Boltzmann calculation.

The BBN "allowed" verdict is therefore trivially true, and the overclosure flag does not contradict the paper.

### BBN robustness and lepton-asymmetry headroom

These are analytic results. We linearized about the server's SM values using the slopes above; they are not server runs. The table gives 95% upper bounds on ΔN_eff relative to th

e SM.

| Data | Yp only | D/H only | Combined |
|---|---|---|---|
| Brief | 0.32 | 0.58 | 0.47 |
| Server | 0.46 | 0.66 | 0.61 |

The server itself reports 0.548. Because the SM D/H sits 2.9σ (brief data) or 4.1σ (server data) low, D/H alone prefers ΔN_eff ≈ 0.26–0.31. The bound therefore shifts by 0.1–0.2 depending on the baseline.

For a joint fit we took dYp/dξ_e = −0.25, ignored any dependence of D/H on ξ_e, and used a 2-dof Δχ² < 5.99:

| Data | Allowed ΔN_eff | ξ_e relation |
|---|---|---|
| Brief | [0.04, 0.48] | ξ_e = 0.0073 + 0.054 ΔN_eff ± 0.029 |
| Server | [0.13, 0.50] | ξ_e = 0.0077 + 0.054 ΔN_eff

# Sterile-neutrino dark matter in 2024-2026: combined BBN and X-ray viability of the (m_s, sin^2 2θ) plane

## Abstract

This study surveyed recent arXiv work on keV sterile-neutrino dark matter. It combined tool-computed BBN observables (Yp, D/H, ΔN_eff) with published X-ray decay-line limits to identify which (m_s, sin^2 2θ) regions remain viable.

**BBN is not a useful constraint on keV dark matter without a lepton asymmetry.**
- Along the non-resonant Dodelson-Widrow (DW) dark-matter line, ΔN_eff is between 1e-4 and 1.1e-2, and the BBN Δχ^2 relative to the Standard Model is below 0.15.
- The overclosure bound is 40 to about 5000 times stronger than BBN over 1-100 keV.

**DW production cannot supply all of the dark matter.**
- X-ray limits exclude it. These are NuSTAR, quoted as sin^2 2θ ≲ 1e-12 at 6-40 keV, and INTEGRAL/SPI, quoted as ≲ 3e-14 above 40 keV.
- Structure formation independently excludes the masses where DW could otherwise survive.
- At 7.1 keV the XRISM-only verdict depends on which DW relic normalization is used. The server's normalization differs from the published fit by a factor of 10-17 in mixing.

**What survives requires non-oscillation production or very small mixing.**
- Shi-Fuller resonant production with a lepton asymmetry L ≳ 0.5 at T > 20 MeV is quoted as viable at m_s ≳ 10 keV and sin^2 2θ ≲ 1e-14 (arXiv:2507.18752). The available server cannot test this: it caps L at 0.1.
- Flavor-dependent asymmetries and reheating production open further regions. Those claims rest on abstracts only.

## Background

The main recent combined analysis is Vogel, Garcia Escudero, Froustey and Abazajian (arXiv:2507.18752, 2025), who revisit Shi-Fuller resonant production. The full text was read, and states:
- "lepton asymmetries L≳0.5 at high temperatures open significant viable parameter space in the m_s≳10 keV and sin^2(2θ)≲10^-14 regime".
- That region is compatible with NuSTAR ("sin^2(2θ)≲10^-12 in the 6–40 keV mass range").
- It is also compatible with INTEGRAL/SPI ("exclude lifetimes below ∼10^20 s at 95% CL [corresponding to sin^2(2θ)≲3×10^-14] in the ≳40 keV mass regime").
- The structure-formation bounds used are m_th > 8.4 keV (galaxy counts, 95% CL) and m_th > 8.5 keV (counts plus strong lensing). The paper also cites a Lyman-alpha preference of m_th = 4.1 (+33.3/−1.5) keV.
- The paper states that "the original DW mechanism is ruled out as producing the entirety of the dark matter".

Three further papers were confirmed to exist by metadata lookup. Only their abstracts were read, so their claims are reported here as abstract-level statements without numerical ranges:
- **Gorbunov, Kalashnikov and Krugan (arXiv:2502.17374, 2025).** Lepton asymmetry spread unequally over flavors can mitigate BBN limits on mixing and mass, through cancellation of flavor asymmetries. The brief notes this works best with inverted ordering. It gives colder spectra that reopen lighter masses.
- **Gorbunov and Kalashnikov (arXiv:2609.31340, 2026).** A high lepton flavor asymmetry saturates resonant production. The board's summary of the abstract is that this leaves a window of about two decades in sin^2 2θ. The concern that this ID was hallucinated is resolved: the paper is real.
- **Cline and Xu (arXiv:2601.03346, 2026).** Cold sterile-neutrino dark matter can be produced by inflaton decays during reheating, with branching ratio ≲ 1e-4. This populates mixings too small for oscillation production and below current X-ray limits.

On the X-ray side, two recent papers were found:
- **XRISM Resolve (arXiv:2510.24560).** This stacked 3.75 Ms on ten clusters over 2.5-15 keV and found no unidentified lines.
- **NuSTAR stray-light analysis (Krivonos, Barinov, Mukhin and Gorbunov, arXiv:2405.17861).** This used 11 years of data and set 95% CL limits for m_s = 6-40 keV.

Baseline references used:
- The Abazajian review (arXiv:1705.01837), for the published DW relic fit.
- Viel et al. (astro-ph/0501562), for the DW-to-thermal mass mapping.
- Merle (arXiv:1702.08430), as a pre-2024 review.

No citable arXiv source was found for 2024-2026 eROSITA or INTEGRAL/SPI line limits. The eROSITA statement in the brief came from a non-citable web snippet.

## Results

### Tool capabilities and assumptions

The sterile-neutrino server computes Yp, D/H and Li7 from a fit to the PRyMordial BBN network, accurate to better than 0.3%. Its only BBN input is ΔN_eff.

| Item | Server setting |
|---|---|
| N_eff validity range | 2.044-6.044 |
| ω_b h^2 validity range | 0.019-0.0257 |
| τ_n validity range | 866.4-890.4 s |
| Mass validity | m_s below about 100 keV; at m_s ≥ 1 MeV decay injection is not modelled |
| Yp data | 0.2449 ± 0.004 (Aver+ 2021) |
| D/H data | (2.547 ± 0.025)e-5 (Cooke+ 2018) |
| N_eff data | Planck 2.99 ± 0.17 |
| Exclusion rule | Δχ^2 > 3.84 relative to the SM |

The server's data values differ from the brief's Yp = 0.245 ± 0.003 and D/H = (2.53 ± 0.03)e-5.

Two production modes are offered:
- **DW (non-resonant).**
- **Shi-Fuller (SF, resonant).** Its ΔN_eff is a heuristic set to 0.1 times the DW value, and its relic density is a fitting formula in L. The lepton asymmetry is not fed into the BBN network.

### BBN versus the DW plane

A 100 × 100 DW scan covered m_s = 1-100 keV and sin^2 2θ = 1e-15 to 1e-6. It showed that BBN excludes only large mixing.

| m_s | BBN exclusion starts above sin^2 2θ = |
|---|---|
| 1 keV | 3.5e-7 |
| 3.7 keV | 1.2e-7 |
| 7 keV | 8.1e-8 |
| 13.5 keV | 4.3e-8 |
| 50 keV | 1.5e-8 |
| 100 keV | 1e-8 |

The server's Ω_s h^2 = 0.12 contour lies far below these thresholds:

| m_s (keV) | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 | 7.1 | 10 | 20 | 50 | 100 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| sin^2 2θ on DM line | 8.7e-9 | 2.5e-9 | 1.2e-9 | 4.8e-10 | 2.55e-10 | 1.37e-10 | 3.9e-11 | 7.6e-12 | 2.2e-12 |

Along this line ΔN_eff is 1e-4 to 1.1e-2 and |Δχ^2_BBN| < 0.15. Overclosure is therefore 40 times (1 keV) to about 5000 times (100 keV) stronger than BBN. The entire DW dark-matter line and everything below it are BBN-allowed.

[[FIGURE 8]]

Figure 8 shows the DW exclusion plot from this scan: the BBN-excluded region at large mixing and the overclosure region, in the (m_s, sin^2 2θ) plane.

Representative points are listed below, with σ values relative to the brief's data.

| Point | ΔN_eff | Yp | D/H | Δχ^2 | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SM, N_eff = 3.044 | 0 | 0.246815 (+0.6σ) | 2.4433e-5 (−2.9σ) | 0 | baseline |
| 7.1 keV, 3e-10 | negligible | 0.24684 | 2.4440e-5 | −0.024 | allowed |
| 1 keV, 3e-7 | 0.387 | 0.25193 (+2.3σ) | 2.5718e-5 (+1.4σ) | 0.44 | allowed |
| 10 keV, 1e-7 | 0.813 | 0.25730 (+4.1σ) | 2.7145e-5 (+6.2σ) | 13.4 | excluded |
| 3 keV, 3e-7 | 0.931 | 0.25874 (+4.6σ) | 2.7540e-5 (+7.5σ) | 19.3 | excluded |

The 1 keV point is allowed despite Yp sitting at +2.3σ. The reason is that the SM D/H sits low, so extra radiation improves the D/H fit and offsets the Yp penalty.

[[FIGURE 6]]

Figure 6 shows the server's BBN response to N_eff. From it:
- BBN alone gives ΔN_eff < 0.548 at 95%.
- The slopes are dYp/dN_eff = 0.0135 and d(D/H × 1e5)/dN_eff = 0.331.

A separate server cross-check used the BEST short-baseline point (m_s = 1.14 eV, sin^2 2θ = 0.42). It gave:
- ΔN_eff = 1, Yp = 0.25956, D/H = 2.777e-5 and Δχ^2 = 23.1, so the point is excluded.
- 6.2σ tension with Planck N_eff, and 33σ at CMB-S4.

### BBN robustness: data baseline and lepton asymmetry

These are analytic results, not server runs. They linearize the slopes above about the server SM values. Bounds are 95% upper limits on ΔN_eff, with Δχ^2 = 3.84 against the SM; values in brackets are against the best fit.

| Data set | Yp only | D/H only | Combined |
|---|---|---|---|
| Brief's data | 0.32 | 0.58 [0.44] | 0.47 [0.37] |
| Server's data | 0.46 | 0.66 [0.46] | 0.61 [0.43] |

The server itself reports 0.548. Because the SM D/H is 2.9σ (brief) to 4.1σ (server) low, D/H alone prefers ΔN_eff ≈ 0.26-0.31. The bound therefore moves by 0.1-0.2 depending on the baseline.

The joint (ΔN_eff, ξ_e) bound used dYp/dξ_e = −0.25, assumed D/H independent of ξ_e, and applied 2-dof Δχ^2 = 5.99.

| Data set | Allowed ΔN_eff | Allowed ξ_e |
|---|---|---|
| Brief's data | [0.04, 0.48] | 0.0073 + 0.054 ΔN_eff ± 0.029 |
| Server's data | [0.13, 0.50] | 0.0077 + 0.054 ΔN_eff ± 0.039 |

Overall this gives |ξ_e| ≲ 0.03-0.06. A positive ξ_e of about 0.03 compensates a ΔN_eff of about 0.5 in Yp. Two caveats affect the ξ_e headroom available to Shi-Fuller scenarios:
- The SM D/H baseline depends on the choice of d(p,γ)3He rate.
- Neglecting dD/H/dξ_e biases the joint contour.

### Shi-Fuller tool tests

SF-mode runs at m_s = 10, 20 and 30 keV with sin^2 2θ = 1e-14 gave ΔN_eff ≈ 1e-8 and BBN Δχ^2 = 0. At 20 keV the outputs were Yp = 0.24682 and D/H = 2.4433e-5.

| L | Ω_s h^2 at 10 keV | at 20 keV | at 30 keV |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1e-3 | 0.122 | 0.490 | 1.10 |
| 0.1 | 1.22 | 4.90 | 11.0 |

All of these points are flagged as overclosing. None of this tests the claims of arXiv:2507.18752, for four reasons:
- The tool caps L at 0.1, while the paper needs L ≳ 0.5.
- Its SF ΔN_eff is a heuristic.
- ξ_e does not enter Yp.
- Its relic density is a fitting formula, not a Boltzmann calculation.

The "BBN-allowed" verdict is trivially true here and is not supporting evidence.

### X-ray decay rate and limits

The server's radiative decay rate agrees with Γ = 1.38e-32 s^-1 (sin^2 2θ/1e-10)(m_s/keV)^5 to within about 1.5%:
- At 7.1 keV and 1e-10 it gives 2.46e-28 s^-1 (formula 2.49e-28), with E = 3.55 keV and lifetime 4.07e27 s.
- At 20 keV and 1e-12 it gives 4.36e-28 s^-1 (formula 4.42e-28), with E = 10 keV.

Equation 2 of arXiv:2405.17861 gives 1.36×10^-22 (m_s/keV)^5 sin^2 2θ s^-1, which equals 1.36e-32 s^-1 at sin^2 2θ = 1e-10, consistent with the above. Whole-halo fluxes at 7.1 keV and 1e-10 are:
- 4.68 ph/s/cm^2 for the Milky Way centre.
- 6.89e-4 ph/s/cm^2 for M31.
- 3.55e-5 ph/s/cm^2 for Perseus.

The tool's built-in limits (NuSTAR M31 from Roach+2020, and XMM blank-sky from Dessert+2020) exclude both test points.

**XRISM and the 3.55 keV line.** The XRISM abstract gives a 3σ limit Γ ∼ 1.0e-27 s^-1 at m_s ∼ 7.1 keV. This is "3−4 times lower than the one derived by Hitomi ... but still 5 times higher than the XMM-Newton detection reported by Bulbul et al. (2014)". The line is therefore constrained but not ruled out. Scaling the rate gives sin^2 2θ ≲ 4e-10 at 7.1 keV. This is our conversion, not a quoted value.

**NuSTAR.** arXiv:2405.17861 sets 95% limits for 6-40 keV. Its observed limits are stronger than expected at 8-9 and 23-25 keV, and it reports a known instrumental excess at 40 keV. Two problems prevented reading numerical values from it:
- Fig. 3 was missing from the HTML rendering.
- The Fig. 1 image was downloaded but could not be digitized with the available tools.

Per-mass NuSTAR entries therefore rest on the secondary summary in arXiv:2507.18752 (≲ 1e-12 across 6-40 keV).

[[FIGURE 15]]

Figure 15 is the Fig. 1 image retrieved from arXiv:2405.17861. No numbers in this report are read from it.

The resulting limit table is below. It was cross-checked with the server's line tool, and is 95% CL unless noted.

| m_s | Limit on sin^2 2θ | Server check |
|---|---|---|
| 7.1 keV | XRISM ≲ 4e-10 (3σ, derived); NuSTAR ≲ 1e-12 | Built-in tables exclude 1e-10 |
| 10 keV | NuSTAR ≲ 1e-12 | At 1e-12: Γ = 1.36e-29 s^-1, E = 5 keV, lifetime 7.35e28 s; not excluded by the tool's tables |
| 20 keV | NuSTAR ≲ 1e-12 | Built-in tables exclude 1e-12, so the tool's table is stronger than the summary value here |
| 40 keV | NuSTAR upper edge (instrumental excess); SPI ≲ 3e-14 above it | none |
| 50 keV | SPI ≲ 3e-14 | At 3e-14: Γ = 1.28e-27 s^-1, E = 25 keV, lifetime 7.84e26 s (2.48e19 yr); not excluded |

Warning: the SPI quote equates "lifetimes below ∼10^20 s" with sin^2 2θ ≲ 3e-14. That is inconsistent with the computed lifetime of 7.84e26 s at that mixing. The tool's lifetime in years (2.48e19 yr) is close to 1e20, which suggests the quoted unit may be years. If so, the SPI ceiling tightens as m_s^-5 rather than staying flat. This is unresolved without the primary SPI paper.

### DW relic normalization and the thermal-equivalent mass

The server's DW relic density scales as Ω_s h^2 = 0.1 (sin^2 2θ/1e-9)(m_s/3 keV)^1.8. Spot checks:
- 3 keV at 1e-9 gives 0.100.
- 10 keV at 1e-9 gives 0.873, a ratio of 8.73, which equals (10/3)^1.8.
- 1 keV at 1e-8 gives 0.138.

The mass exponent matches the brief's formula, but the normalization is three times higher than the brief's.

The published fit in arXiv:1705.01837, Eq. 37, is

m_s ≈ 3.40 keV (sin^2 2θ/1e-8)^-0.615 (Ω_DM/0.26)^0.5 × 0.527 erfc[−1.15 (T_QCD/170 MeV)^2.15].

Inverted by hand, it places the DM line as follows.

| m_s (keV) | 3 | 7.1 | 10 | 20 | 50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Published fit | 1.23e-8 | 3.0e-9 | 1.73e-9 | 5.6e-10 | 1.26e-10 |
| Server (Ω h^2 = 0.119-0.120) | 1.2e-9 | 2.55e-10 | 1.37e-10 | 3.9e-11 | 7.6e-12 |

The QCD-era uncertainty (T_QCD = 150-200 MeV) moves the published line by about +10%/−7%. The published line needs 10-17 times more mixing than the server and 3.4-5.5 times more than the brief's formula. It also differs in shape: Ω ∝ m^2 (sin^2 2θ)^1.23.

At 7.1 keV, measured against XRISM (≲ 4e-10):
- The server line (2.55e-10) survives.
- The brief's line (7.65e-10) is excluded.
- The published line (3.0e-9) is excluded, by about 7.5 times.

Taking the published fit as the reference, XRISM alone excludes DW dark matter at 7.1 keV. Server-based DW statements are not conservative.

**Thermal-equivalent mass.** Using m_s = 4.43 keV (m_th/keV)^(4/3) (Viel et al. 2005; not quoted verbatim from the downloaded text), the DW line maps as follows.

| m_s (keV) | 3 | 7.1 | 10 | 20 | 50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| m_th (keV) | 0.75 | 1.42 | 1.84 | 3.10 | 6.16 |

The structure-formation bounds then translate into mass requirements:
- Lyman-alpha m_th > 4 (6) keV requires m_s > 28 (48) keV.
- Satellite counts (m_th > 8.4 keV) require m_s > 76 keV.

At m_s ≥ 28 keV the DW line sits at about 3e-10 (published) or about 1e-11 (server). Both are far above the NuSTAR and SPI ceilings, so the surviving DW mass interval is empty under all three normalizations. This is robust to the 10-30% differ
